李白: Li Bai (701–762), courtesy name Taibai, styled Qinglian Jushi, was the preeminent Romantic poet of the High Tang dynasty, revered as the 'Poet Immortal.' Known for his bold, ethereal style and vivid imagination, he excelled in seven-character songs and quatrains, often expressing his aspirations and frustrations. Together with Du Fu, he is celebrated as one of the 'Li-Du' duo, occupying a pinnacle position in Chinese literary history.
杜甫: Du Fu (712-770), courtesy name Zimei, was a preeminent realist poet of the Tang Dynasty. Living through the transition from the Tang's zenith to its decline, his poetry is characterized by its profound depth and social concern, earning him the titles of 'Poet-Historian' and 'Sage of Poetry.' Often paired with Li Bai as 'Li-Du,' his work remains a cornerstone of Chinese literature.
王维: Wang Wei, courtesy name Mojie, was a preeminent poet, painter, and musician of the High Tang Dynasty. Known as the 'Poet Buddha' for his profound Buddhist insights, his works are celebrated for their serene, picturesque quality, often described as 'painting in poetry and poetry in painting.' His masterpieces, such as 'Deer Park,' solidified his status as a master of landscape and pastoral poetry.
孟浩然: Meng Haoran (689-740), a native of Xiangyang during the High Tang Dynasty, was a representative poet of the Shanshui (landscape and garden) school. Often mentioned alongside Wang Wei as 'Wang-Meng,' his poetry is celebrated for its natural, serene, and transcendent style, earning him a significant place in Tang poetry with masterpieces like 'Spring Dawn' and 'Mooring on the Jiande River.'
白居易: Bai Juyi (772-846), courtesy name Letian, styled Xiangshan Jushi, was a great realist poet of the mid-Tang Dynasty. Advocating that poetry should reflect social reality, his style is renowned for its clarity and accessibility. Famous for works like 'Song of Everlasting Regret' and 'Song of the Pipa', he is paired with Yuan Zhen as 'Yuan-Bai' and holds a significant position in literary history.
王昌龄: Wang Changling (c. 698–756), courtesy name Shaobo, was a prominent frontier poet of the High Tang period, celebrated as a master of the seven-character quatrain. Renowned for his majestic frontier poems and elegant palace laments, his representative works include "Border Song" and "Army March," securing his status as a peerless figure alongside Gao Shi and Wang Zhihuan.
杜牧: Du Mu (803-852) was a native of Jingzhao Wannian during the late Tang Dynasty, courtesy name Muzhi, often referred to as 'Little Du'. Known for his bold, elegant, and incisive poetic style, he excelled in seven-character quatrains, with representative works such as 'Mooring on the Qinhuai River' and 'Rhapsody on Epang Palace'. Together with Li Shangyin, he is known as one of the 'Little Li-Du', holding a significant position in the poetry of the late Tang.
李商隐: Li Shangyin (c. 813–858), courtesy name Yishan, pseudonym Yuxisheng, was a preeminent poet of the late Tang Dynasty. Renowned for his ornate, intricate style and poignant, enigmatic 'Untitled Poems', he is celebrated for his profound emotional depth and is often paired with Du Mu as one of the 'Little Li-Du', holding a distinguished position in the history of Chinese poetry.
柳宗元: Liu Zongyuan (773-819), courtesy name Zihou, was a prominent Tang Dynasty writer known as 'Liu Hedong'. A leader of the Classical Prose Movement alongside Han Yu, he is celebrated for his profound and elegant literary style. His works, particularly the 'Eight Records of Yongzhou' and the poem 'River Snow' written during his exile, hold a distinguished place in the history of Chinese literature.
刘禹锡: Liu Yuxi (772–842), courtesy name Mengde, was a prominent poet and philosopher of the mid-to-late Tang Dynasty. Despite a turbulent political career marked by frequent exiles, his poetry is celebrated for its bold and vigorous style, often reflecting on history and social concerns; known for works like 'Ode to My Humble Abode' and 'Bamboo Branch Songs,' he is paired with Bai Juyi as 'Liu-Bai' and holds a significant status in the history of Chinese poetry.
张继: Zhang Ji, courtesy name Yisun, was a mid-Tang Dynasty poet and a successful candidate in the imperial examination during the Tianbao era. Known for his elegant and refined poetic style, he excelled in travel poetry, and his masterpiece 'Night Mooring at Maple Bridge' remains one of the most celebrated works in Chinese literary history.
王之涣: Wang Zhihuan (688–742), courtesy name Jiling, was a renowned poet of the High Tang period. Celebrated for his frontier poetry characterized by a grand and profound style, his masterpieces such as "Ascending Stork Tower" and "Liangzhou Ci" are widely acclaimed, cementing his status as an iconic representative of the High Tang poetic spirit.
孟郊: Meng Jiao (751–814), courtesy name Dongye, was a mid-to-late Tang dynasty poet and a close friend of Han Yu, known as a representative of the 'bitter chanting' style. Having achieved success in the imperial examinations only late in life, his poetry is characterized by a stark and rugged style, often focusing on the suffering of the common people and his own personal hardships; his famous work 'Song of the Wanderer' secures his unique status in the history of Chinese poetry.
贾岛: Jia Dao (779-843), courtesy name Langxian, was a mid-to-late Tang Dynasty poet who spent his early years as a Buddhist monk. Renowned for his meticulous and painstaking poetic craft, he is famous for the anecdote of 'tuiqiao' (pushing or knocking) and his austere, refined style, often paired with Meng Jiao as 'Jiao Han Dao Shou' (Meng's coldness and Jia's thinness).
苏轼: Su Shi (1037-1101), courtesy name Zizhan, pseudonym Dongpo Jushi, was a prominent literary figure and leader of the Northern Song Dynasty. One of the 'Three Sus' alongside his father and brother, he is celebrated as one of the 'Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song' and a pioneer of the bold and unconstrained style in Ci poetry. His profound mastery of literature, calligraphy, and painting, exemplified by works like 'Ode to the Red Cliff', secures his exalted status in Chinese literary history.
辛弃疾: Xin Qiji, courtesy name You'an and art name Jiaxuan, was a native of Jinan during the Southern Song Dynasty. A preeminent representative of the "bold and unconstrained" style of Ci poetry, he is often paired with Su Shi as "Su-Xin" and holds a towering position in literary history. His works, such as "Yongyu Le: Gazing from Jingkou Beigu Pavilion," are known for their heroic spirit and themes of patriotism and the longing to reclaim lost territories.
李清照: Li Qingzhao (1084-1155), known by her art name Yi'an Jushi, was a preeminent poet of the Southern Song Dynasty and is celebrated as the greatest female poet in Chinese history. Renowned for her delicate and graceful style, her early works focus on romantic longing, while her later poems reflect the sorrow of exile and national loss; her masterpieces include 'Sheng Sheng Man', 'Ru Meng Ling', and the prose 'Jin Shi Lu Hou Xu'.
柳永: Liu Yong, originally named Sanbian with the courtesy name Qiqing, was a native of Chong'an during the Northern Song Dynasty and a preeminent representative of the Wanyue (Delicate) school of Ci poetry. He pioneered the "manci" (long lyric) form, using descriptive techniques to depict urban prosperity and the hardships of travel, with "Yulinling" being one of his masterpieces. Holding a prestigious position in literary history, he profoundly influenced the development of Song lyrics, famously noted that "wherever there is a well, Liu's lyrics are sung."
岳飞: Yue Fei (1103-1142), courtesy name Pengju, was a renowned Southern Song Dynasty general and national hero who fought against the Jin. His poetry is characterized by a heroic and tragic style, best exemplified by 'Man Jiang Hong', which expresses his unwavering loyalty and ambition to recover lost territories, earning him a revered status in literary history as a patriotic poet.
陆游: Lu You (1125–1210), courtesy name Wuguan and pseudonym Fangweng, was a distinguished patriotic poet and historian of the Southern Song Dynasty. A staunch advocate for resisting the Jin dynasty to reclaim lost territories, his poetry is celebrated for its vigorous, heroic spirit as well as its delicate lyricism. Famous for works such as "To My Son" and "Expressing My Indignation," he is revered in Chinese literary history as a master of patriotic poetry.
范仲淹: Fan Zhongyan (989-1052), courtesy name Xiwen, was a prominent statesman and writer of the Northern Song Dynasty. A leader of the 'Qingli Reforms', he is best remembered for the profound sentiment 'to be the first to worry about the world's troubles and the last to enjoy its pleasures' from his masterpiece 'Memorial to Yueyang Tower'. His literary works, characterized by a solemn and poignant style, occupy a pivotal position in the history of Song Dynasty literature.
欧阳修: Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072), courtesy name Yongshu, pseudonyms Zuiweng and Liuyi Jushi, was a prominent Northern Song statesman and writer, and one of the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song. He led the movement for classical prose, known for his fresh, accessible poetry and poignant lyrics, with masterpieces like 'Account of the Old Drunkard's Pavilion' and 'Ode on the Autumn Sound'. As a leading literary figure of his time, he exerted a profound influence on later Chinese literature.
晏殊: Yan Shu (991-1055), courtesy name Tongshu, was a prominent Northern Song Dynasty official who rose to the rank of Chancellor and is celebrated as the 'Chancellor Poet.' A pioneer of the Song ci genre, he is renowned for his elegant and subtle poetic style, with his masterpiece 'Huanxi Sha' remaining a timeless classic in Chinese literature.
秦观: Qin Guan (1049-1100), courtesy name Shaoyou, known as Huaihai Jushi, was a prominent poet of the Northern Song Dynasty and one of the 'Four Scholars of the Su Gate.' Renowned for his delicate and poignant Ci poetry, he is considered a master of the Wanyue (graceful and restrained) school, with famous works such as 'Que Qiao Xian'.
姜夔: Jiang Kui (1155–1209), courtesy name Yaozhang and pseudonym Baishi Daoren, was a prominent poet and musician of the Southern Song Dynasty. Renowned for his mastery of musical rhythm and self-composed melodies, his poetry is celebrated for its elegant, refined, and ethereal style, exemplified by works such as "Yangzhou Man," which secured his unique status in the history of Song Ci poetry.
周邦彦: Zhou Bangyan was a prominent poet of the late Northern Song Dynasty, known by his courtesy name Meicheng and pseudonym Qingzhen Jushi. A master of musical rhythm and descriptive imagery, his works are celebrated for their rigorous structure and refined language, earning him the title of the 'Grandmaster of the Formalist School' and leaving a profound legacy in Chinese poetry; his representative works include 'Lanling Wang' and 'Sumuzhe'.
佚名: This is a collection of classical poems by unknown authors, selected from anthologies such as 'Classic of Poetry,' 'Complete Tang Poems,' and 'Song Ci'.
曹操: Cao Cao (155–220), courtesy name Mengde, was a prominent statesman, strategist, and poet of the late Eastern Han dynasty, as well as the founder and leader of the Jian'an literature. His poetry, characterized by a grand yet melancholic style, often utilizes traditional Yuefu themes to express his political ambitions for unification and to document the suffering of the people during wartime, with representative works including 'Short Song Style' and 'Viewing the Blue Sea', marking his significant status in the history of Chinese poetry.
李煜: Li Yu (937-978), courtesy name Chongguang, was the last ruler of the Southern Tang dynasty during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Known as the 'Emperor of Ci Poetry,' he transformed the genre by shifting its focus from romantic themes to profound expressions of national loss and personal sorrow. His works, such as 'Yu Mei Ren' and 'Xiang Jian Huan,' are celebrated for their natural language and deep emotional resonance, marking a pivotal transition in the history of Chinese poetry.
温庭筠: Wen Tingyun (c. 812–866), courtesy name Feiqing, was a prominent poet and lyricist of the late Tang Dynasty, often mentioned alongside Li Shangyin as the pair "Wen-Li." Renowned for his musicality and ornate, sensuous style, he is celebrated as the founding father of the "Huajian" (Among the Flowers) school of poetry, exerting a profound influence on the development of Chinese lyric poetry (ci).
韦庄: Wei Zhuang (836-910), courtesy name Duanji, was a prominent poet and lyricist during the late Tang Dynasty and the Five Dynasties period. As a key figure of the 'Huajian' (Among the Flowers) school, he is celebrated for his elegant lyrics and his famous narrative poem 'Lament of the Woman of Qin,' holding a significant place in the history of Chinese poetry.
马致远: Ma Zhiyuan was a prominent Yuan dynasty playwright and sanqu poet, known by the sobriquet Dongli and honored as the 'Master of Qu'. His works are characterized by a bold and melancholic style, with masterpieces like 'Tianjingsha: Autumn Thoughts' remaining legendary in the history of Yuan drama.
张养浩: Zhang Yanghao (1270-1329), courtesy name Ximeng, pseudonym Yunzhuang, was a renowned Yuan dynasty sanqu poet and statesman. Famous for his sanqu masterpieces such as 'Shanpo Yang: Thoughts on Tongguan', his work is characterized by a melancholic and profound style that deeply reflects the hardships of the people, securing him a prominent place in the history of Yuan poetry.
徐再思: Xu Zaisi, courtesy name Deke and pseudonym Tianzhai, was a renowned Yuan dynasty sanqu poet. Often paired with Qiao Ji as 'Qiao-Xu', his works are celebrated for their elegant and lyrical style, particularly in themes of romance and longing. His representative works, such as 'Shuixianzi: Seeking Plum Blossoms', hold a significant place in the history of Yuan sanqu poetry.
宋方壶: Qiao Ji was a renowned Yuan dynasty sanqu poet, also known by his courtesy name Mengfu and pseudonyms Shenghe and Xingxing Daoren. His works are characterized by an elegant and refined style, distinguishing him among his contemporaries; he is highly regarded in the history of Yuan literature, with notable works such as 'Two Generations of Marriage'.
张可久: Zhang Kejiu, courtesy name Xiaoshan, was a prominent Yuan dynasty qu poet, often paired with Qiao Ji as 'Zhang-Qiao'. His works, which frequently depict natural scenery and the reclusive life, are renowned for their elegant and refined style, establishing him as a leading figure of the 'Qingli' (Clear and Elegant) school in the history of Yuan qu.
纳兰性德: Nalan Xingde, courtesy name Rongruo and art name Lengjia Shanren, was a renowned Manchu Ci poet during the Kangxi period of the Qing Dynasty, ranked among the 'Three Great Ci Poets of the Qing.' His works are celebrated for their sincerity and naturalness, featuring a delicate and melancholic style that often explores themes of mourning, frontier life, and travel weariness, with 'Yinshui Ci' being his representative collection. Despite his noble background, he passed away at the young age of thirty-one, yet his poetry is highly acclaimed in literary history as being unparalleled since the Northern Song Dynasty.
王建: Wang Jian (c. 767–830), courtesy name Zhongchu, was a prominent mid-Tang dynasty poet often paired with Zhang Ji as 'Zhang-Wang'. Renowned for his yuefu poetry, his style is characterized by freshness and simplicity, with his 'One Hundred Palace Poems' being particularly celebrated for their vivid depiction of court life, securing his significant status in Tang poetry.
马戴: Ma Dai (799-869), courtesy name Yuchen, was a renowned poet of the late Tang Dynasty who served as a magistrate of Longyang and a professor at the Imperial Academy. His poetry is characterized by a melancholic and desolate style, excelling in five-character regulated verse with themes of frontier landscapes and traveler's sorrow; his masterpiece 'Reminiscence of the Chu River' is considered a classic of the late Tang.
元稹: Yuan Zhen, courtesy name Weizhi, was a prominent poet and writer during the mid-Tang Dynasty. Known for his close friendship with Bai Juyi and their joint advocacy of the New Music Bureau movement, they were collectively known as 'Yuan-Bai,' and his accessible poetic style became the hallmark of the 'Yuanhe style.' A significant figure in Tang poetry, his masterpiece 'Five Poems on Parting' remains highly influential in Chinese literary history.
沈佺期: Shen Quanqi (c. 656–714), courtesy name Yunqing, was an influential poet of the early Tang Dynasty. Often paired with Song Zhiwen as "Shen-Song," he played a pivotal role in standardizing the prosody of regulated verse, particularly the seven-character lüshi, significantly paving the way for the poetic flourishing of the High Tang.
韩愈: Han Yu (768-824), courtesy name Tuizhi, was a prominent writer and philosopher of the mid-Tang Dynasty and a leader of the Classical Prose Movement. Known for his vigorous and unconventional poetic style, he is celebrated for works such as 'Written on the Way to Lantian' and is revered in literary history as a master who revitalized classical prose.
杜荀鹤: Du Xunhe (846—904), courtesy name Yanzhi, self-styled Jiuhua Shanren, was a prominent poet of the late Tang Dynasty. His poetry often focused on the hardships of the common people with an accessible style; his representative works include 'The Widow in the Mountains,' and his collection is known as the 'Tangfeng Ji.'
朱庆余: Zhu Qingyu (courtesy name Kejiu, from Yuezhou) was a representative poet of the Mid-Tang Dynasty who gained recognition from Zhang Ji and passed the imperial examination. His poetry is characterized by a graceful and delicate style, with his 'boudoir grievance' poems, such as 'Presenting to Vice-Minister Zhang,' being particularly renowned; he holds a significant place in Tang poetry, often praised for his keen literary insight.
许浑: Xu Hun (791-858), courtesy name Yonghui, was a prominent late Tang Dynasty poet from Danyang, Runzhou, who served as a regional governor. Known for his melancholic and elegant style, he excelled in themes of historical reflection and travel, and his collection, 'Dingmao Ji', is named after his residence, Dingmao Bridge.
李益: Li Yi (748—827), courtesy name Junyu, was a prominent mid-Tang dynasty poet from Guzang, Longxi (modern-day Wuwei, Gansu), who once served as Secretary of the Imperial Library. Renowned for his frontier poetry characterized by a bold and melancholic style, his famous work 'Hearing a Flute on Suoxiang City at Night' was widely circulated, marking his significant contribution to the development of Tang frontier verse.
司空曙: Sikong Shu, courtesy name Wenming, was a poet of the Dali period in the Mid-Tang Dynasty and one of the 'Ten Talents of Dali'. Having served as a bureau director, he is known for his elegant and refined style, often expressing themes of travel weariness and leisure, with representative works like 'Staying at Yunyang Inn with Han Shen' securing his unique place in Tang poetry history.
刘长卿: Liu Changqing (c. 709–780), courtesy name Wenfang, was a prominent mid-Tang Dynasty poet who served as an imperial censor and governor of Suizhou. Renowned for his refined five-character poems, he was hailed as the "Great Wall of Five-Character Poetry" and holds a significant place in Tang literary history, with works such as "Staying at the Master's House in Furong Mountain During Snow" being his most celebrated pieces.
卢纶: Lu Lun (c. 737–799), courtesy name Yunyan, was a mid-Tang dynasty poet and one of the 'Ten Talents of the Dali Era.' Having served as a magistrate and imperial censor, he is best known for his frontier poetry characterized by a vigorous and elegant style. His six 'Songs of the Frontier' remain widely celebrated, securing his significant place in the history of Tang poetry.
崔颢: Cui Hao (c. 704–754) was a Tang Dynasty poet from Bianzhou who earned his jinshi degree during the Kaiyuan era. Initially known for a flamboyant style, his later work became bold and vigorous; his masterpiece, 'Yellow Crane Tower,' is considered the finest heptasyllabic regulated verse of the Tang Dynasty, earning him a prestigious place in literary history.
李颀: Li Qi (c. 690–751) was a poet of the High Tang period. Though his courtesy name is unknown, he served as the Magistrate of Xinxiang. Renowned for his vigorous and bold style, he is particularly celebrated for his frontier poetry, farewell poems, and vivid descriptions of music, such as 'Song of Listening to An Wanshan Playing the Piri,' securing his significant status in Tang poetry.
崔涂: Cui Tu was a poet of the late Tang Dynasty, courtesy name Lishan, from Tonglu, Zhejiang. He attained the Jinshi degree during the Guangqi era; his poetry, represented by works like "Spring Evening," is characterized by a melancholic and elegant style, often expressing the sorrow of travel and reflections on a turbulent age. He is recognized as a significant figure in late Tang regulated verse, noted for his profound sense of anxiety.
张祜: Zhang Hu, courtesy name Chengji, was a poet of the middle to late Tang Dynasty. Renowned for his palace-style poetry, he possessed a refined and graceful style, excelling in depictions of court life and frontier landscapes, and is celebrated in the history of Tang poetry as the master of palace verse.
王涯: Wang Ya, courtesy name Guangjin, was a high-ranking official and poet during the middle-to-late Tang Dynasty. Known for his erudition and elegant, refreshing poetic style, he excelled in depicting court life and natural scenery, with works such as his "Gongci" (Palace Poems). He held a notable position in Tang poetry but was ultimately executed due to his involvement in the political factionalism of the Sweet Dew Incident.
张九龄: Zhang Jiuling (678—740), courtesy name Zishou, was a virtuous chancellor and poet during the Kaiyuan Era of the Tang Dynasty. His poetry is characterized by a refined and archaic style, with his twelve 'Ganyu' poems serving as representative works that reflect his profound patriotism and lofty political aspirations. Known as the 'First Man of Lingnan,' he holds a significant position in the history of Tang poetry for his role in bridging different literary eras.
宋之问: Song Zhiwen, courtesy name Yanqing, was a poet of the early Tang Dynasty, active during the reigns of Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Ruizong. Known alongside Shen Quanqi as 'Shen-Song,' he was a pivotal figure in the formalization of the five-character regulated verse, contributing significantly to its metrical maturity with his ornate style. Despite his political disgrace and eventual forced suicide due to his association with the powerful official Wu Sansi, he holds a significant transitional position in the history of Chinese poetry.
高适: Gao Shi (704-765), courtesy name Dafu, was a prominent frontier poet of the High Tang period who served as a military governor. Known for his heroic and vigorous poetic style, his masterpiece 'Song of Yan' depicts the hardships and grandeur of frontier life; he holds a significant position in Tang poetry and is often paired with Cen Shen as 'Gao-Cen'.
钱起: Qian Qi, courtesy name Zhongwen, was a prominent poet of the mid-Tang Dynasty and the leader of the 'Ten Talents of the Dali Era.' His poetry is characterized by its elegant, novel style and profound depth, with a focus on landscape and farewell themes, holding a significant place in the history of Tang poetry.
元结: Yuan Jie, courtesy name Cishan, was a prominent official and poet during the mid-Tang Dynasty. Serving as the Prefect of Daozhou, he was known for his integrity and his poetry, which often focused on the hardships of the people with a rustic and vigorous style. He is a significant pioneer of realist poetry in the Tang Dynasty, renowned for his 'Zhongxing Song' and the anthology 'Qiezhong Ji'.
韩翃: Han Hong, courtesy name Junping, was a prominent mid-Tang Dynasty poet and the leader of the 'Ten Talents of Dali.' Known for his elegant and lyrical style, he excelled in themes of longing and frontier life, most notably his celebrated poem 'Hanshi,' which holds a significant place in the history of Tang poetry.
韦应物: Wei Yingwu (737–792), a mid-Tang dynasty poet, also known by his courtesy name Yibo, served as the Governor of Suzhou, earning him the title 'Wei Suzhou.' His poetry is characterized by its elegant, serene, and minimalist style, particularly in his landscape and pastoral works; often compared to Tao Yuanming as 'Tao-Wei,' he is a pivotal figure in the transition from the High Tang to the Mid-Tang poetic tradition.
岑参: Cen Shen (c. 715–770) was a prominent poet of the High Tang dynasty. Known for his frontier poetry, he served twice in the Western Regions, which inspired his magnificent and vivid style. His representative work, such as 'Song of White Snow in Farewell to Judge Wu Returning to the Capital,' solidified his status alongside Gao Shi as a master of the frontier genre.
严维: Yan Wei, courtesy name Zhengwen, was a mid-Tang Dynasty poet from Shanyin, Yuezhou. Having served as a proofreader in the Imperial Secretariat, he was known for his ornate and elegant poetic style, particularly his celebrated landscape and pastoral poems, which secured his place in the history of Tang poetry.
吴文英: Wu Wenying, courtesy name Junte and art name Mengchuang, was a prominent lyricist of the late Southern Song Dynasty who never held official office. His works are renowned for their ornate diction, profound imagery, and complex structure, making him a master of the 'Gelu School' (Formalist School), with 'Ying Ti Xu' being one of his masterpieces. Characterized by a dense and ethereal style, he is hailed as the 'Li Shangyin of Ci poetry' and has exerted a profound influence on later generations.
晏几道: Yan Jidao was a renowned Ci poet of the late Northern Song Dynasty, styled Shuyuan and known by his pseudonym Xiaoshan, the seventh son of Yan Shu. Following his father's literary tradition, he was celebrated for his deeply sentimental and refined style, with his works compiled in 'Xiaoshan Ci', earning him a significant place in Song poetry as a master of melancholy.
张炎: Zhang Yan was a renowned lyricist from the late Southern Song to the early Yuan Dynasty, with the courtesy name Shuxia and the pseudonym Yutian. He inherited the styles of Zhou Bangyan and Jiang Kui, advocating for 'ethereal clarity' and 'elegant refinement,' and is a key representative of the Formalist school. His lyrics often use objects to express emotions and lament the fall of his nation; he holds a prestigious status in literary history with his theoretical work 'Ciyuan' and collection 'Shanzhong Baiyun Ci'.
贺铸: He Zhu (1052-1125), courtesy name Fanghui, known as Qinghu Yilao, was a prominent poet of the Northern Song Dynasty. His lyrical style blends delicate grace with bold vigor, often incorporating classical allusions. He is best remembered for the line "plum-ripening rain" from his masterpiece "Qing Yu An," earning him the nickname "He Meizi" and securing his significant status in the history of Song poetry.
刘辰翁: Liu Chenweng (1232–1297), courtesy name Huimeng, pseudonym Xuxi, was a prominent patriotic lyricist and man of letters from Ji'an, Jiangxi, during the late Southern Song Dynasty. His ci poetry, characterized by a melancholic and profound style, often expresses deep sorrow for the fallen dynasty and the plight of the displaced, with works like 'Lanling Wang: Seeing off Spring in the Bingzi Year' serving as representative pieces that hold significant status in the history of Song dynasty literature.
周密: Zhou Mi (1232–1298), courtesy name Gongjin, pseudonym Caochuang, was a prominent poet, historian, and bibliographer of the late Southern Song Dynasty. As one of the 'Four Great Ci Poets of the Southern Song,' his works are known for their elegant and refined style, while his prose writings like 'Wulin Jiushi' provide invaluable historical records of the prosperity of Lin'an and the legacy of the Song court.
张元干: Zhang Yuangan (1091–1161), courtesy name Zhongzong, styled Lucuan Jushi, was a patriotic poet of the early Southern Song Dynasty. Known for his bold and impassioned style, he is a key figure in the 'bold and unconstrained' (haofang) school of Southern Song ci poetry, with representative works such as 'Shizhou Man' collected in 'Lucuan Jushi Ci'.
吕渭老: Lü Weilao, courtesy name Shengqiu, was a poet from Jiaxing during the late Northern Song Dynasty. His ci poetry, characterized by a graceful and elegant style, primarily explores themes of melancholy, parting, and the sorrows of travel; though few works survive, they hold a distinct place in the history of Song poetry.
张先: Zhang Xian (990–1078), courtesy name Ziye, was a prominent Northern Song dynasty poet known as 'Zhang Three-Shadows' for the exquisite imagery in his lyrics. Following the style of Liu Yong, he excelled in depicting themes of travel-weariness and feminine sentiment, playing a pivotal role in the transition from short lyrics to longer forms in Song poetry; his representative work includes 'Tianxianzi'.
史达祖: Shi Dazu was a renowned lyric poet of the late Southern Song Dynasty, known by his courtesy name Bangqing and pseudonym Meixi. He excelled in writing object-oriented ci poetry, characterized by exquisite diction and ingenious conception; his collection, 'Meixi Ci', holds a unique position in Southern Song literature and significantly influenced later poetic styles.
蔡伸: Cai Shen (1088-1156), courtesy name Shendao and pseudonym Yougu Jushi, was a poet during the transition from the Northern to Southern Song Dynasty. Having served in various local official positions, his lyrics often express the melancholy of travel and romantic longing, with his collection 'Yougu Ci' securing him a notable place in the history of Song Dynasty poetry.
晁补之: Chao Buzhi (1053–1110) was a prominent Northern Song dynasty writer, courtesy name Wujiu, self-styled Guilaizi. A disciple of Su Shi, he is celebrated as one of the 'Four Scholars of the Su Gate' alongside Huang Tingjian, Qin Guan, and Zhang Lei. Known for his elegant poetry and prose that often expressed his frustrations in official life, his works are collected in the 'Jilei Ji'. He holds a significant position in literary history as a key precursor to the Jiangxi School of poetry.
蒋捷: Jiang Jie (after 1245-1305), courtesy name Shengyu, pseudonym Zhushan, was a poet during the transition from the late Southern Song to the early Yuan Dynasty. His lyrics are characterized by a profound and melancholic style, especially those written during his reclusive life after the fall of the Song, with his masterpiece 'Yu Mei Ren: Listening to the Rain' being the most famous. He is celebrated in the history of Chinese poetry for his collection 'Zhushan Ci', which captures the unique sentiments of the Song loyalists.
周紫芝: Zhou Zizhi (1082–1155) was a prominent poet and lyricist of the mid-Southern Song Dynasty, known by his courtesy name Shaoyin and pseudonym Zhupo Jushi. His poetry is characterized by a clear and natural style, while his lyrics often express themes of homesickness and patriotism; he is well-regarded for his works 'Taicang Timi Ji' and the literary criticism 'Zhupo Shihua'.
张孝祥: Zhang Xiaoxiang (1132–1170), courtesy name Anguo and pseudonym Yuhu Jushi, was an outstanding patriotic poet and calligrapher of the Southern Song Dynasty. His Ci poetry style, inheriting from Su Shi and paving the way for Xin Qiji, is renowned for being bold and vigorous, with his masterpiece 'Nian Nu Jiao: Passing Lake Dongting' showcasing his noble character and broad mind. He holds a prominent position in the Southern Song literary world as a key founder and representative of the 'Bold and Unrestrained' school.
袁去华: Yuan Quhua, a jinshi scholar during the Shaoxing reign of the Southern Song Dynasty, was a renowned poet known by his courtesy name Xuanqing and pseudonym Shizhai. His lyrical style is elegant and graceful, heavily influenced by Su Shi and Huang Tingjian, with a focus on themes of travel and personal reflection; he holds a significant place in the history of Song poetry, with works including 'Shizhai Leigao' and 'Yuan Xuanqing Ci'.
刘克庄: Liu Kezhuang (1187–1269), courtesy name Qianfu and art name Houcun, was a prominent writer, historian, and leader of the 'Rivers and Lakes' (Jianghu) poetry school during the late Southern Song Dynasty. His poetry is characterized by a bold style that reflects social reality and patriotic sentiments, while his ci poetry, influenced by Xin Qiji, is known for its grand momentum. As a towering figure in late Southern Song literature, his works like 'The Complete Collection of Mr. Houcun' and 'Houcun's Remarks on Poetry' hold significant status in literary history and criticism.
卢祖皋: Lu Zugao (1174–1224), courtesy name Shenzhi, pseudonym Pujiang, was a native of Yongjia during the Southern Song Dynasty. After passing the imperial examination in 1199, he became known for his collection 'Pujiang Ci,' characterized by an elegant and delicate style that often explored themes of travel weariness and romantic longing, establishing him as a significant figure in Southern Song poetry.
祖咏: Zu Yong (699—746) was a poet from Luoyang during the High Tang Dynasty. A jinshi scholar of the Kaiyuan era and a close friend of Wang Wei, he is celebrated for his elegant landscape and pastoral poetry. His masterpiece, 'Gazing at the Remaining Snow on Zhongnan Mountain,' is renowned for its painterly quality, securing his place in the history of Tang poetry.
李之仪: Li Zhiyi (1048-1117), courtesy name Duanshu, known as Guxi Jushi, was a Northern Song dynasty poet from Wudi, Cangzhou. A disciple of Su Shi, he is renowned for his graceful and elegant ci poetry, most notably "Bu Suan Zi: I Live at the Head of the Yangtze River," which holds a significant place in the history of Song dynasty literature; his works are collected in the "Guxi Jushi Qianhou Ji."
范成大: Fan Chengda (1126-1193), courtesy name Zhineng and pseudonym Shihu Jushi, was one of the Four Great Poets of the Southern Song Dynasty. Renowned for his pastoral poetry, his work 'Si Shi Tian Yuan Za Xing' vividly depicts rural life and the hardships of the people; his elegant and lyrical style holds a significant place in the history of Song poetry.
韩元吉: Han Yuanji (1118–c. 1186), courtesy name Wujiu and pseudonym Nanjian, was a prominent official and poet of the Southern Song Dynasty. Rising to the rank of Minister of Personnel, he was celebrated for his elegant and vigorous poetic style, particularly in the ci genre, and is recognized as the representative figure of the 'Nanjian style' in literary history, with works such as 'Seeing Off Lu Wuguan to Fujian' being highly regarded.
王沂孙: Wang Yisun, courtesy name Shengyu and pseudonym Bishan, was a poet active from the late Southern Song to the early Yuan dynasty, recognized as one of the 'Four Great Masters of the Late Song'. He is celebrated for his sophisticated and evocative object-oriented ci poetry, which often carries profound sentiments of national loss, with representative works including 'Qi Tian Le: Cicada' and his collection 'Bishan Yuefu'.
刘方平: Liu Fangping, a native of Luoyang, Henan during the Tang Dynasty, was a renowned scholar of the Tianbao era and a close friend of Yuan Dexiu. He lived as a recluse and never entered officialdom; his poetic style is elegant and natural, excelling in depicting boudoir sentiments and natural scenes. His representative works, such as 'Moonlit Night' and 'Spring Complaint,' are known for their profound and delicate imagery, earning him a distinct place in Tang poetry.
仲殊: Zhongshu was a Northern Song dynasty monk, originally named Zhang Hui, with the courtesy name Shili. A close friend of Su Shi, he was renowned for his exquisite and elegant lyrical style, often depicting landscapes and Zen philosophy, which earned him a distinct place in Northern Song poetry; his representative work includes 'Nanke Zi: Remembering the Past'.
刘过: Liu Guo (1154-1206), courtesy name Gaizhi and pseudonym Longzhou Daoren, was a prominent poet and lyricist of the Southern Song Dynasty, known for his fervent patriotism and anti-Jin stance. Living his life as a commoner without holding official office, his works are characterized by a bold and unrestrained style; he frequently exchanged poems with masters like Lu You and Xin Qiji, securing a significant place in the history of Song Dynasty poetry.
叶梦得: Ye Mengde (1077—1148), courtesy name Shaoyun, styled Shilinjushi, was a poet and official during the transition from the Northern to the Southern Song Dynasty. His lyrical style shifted from the delicate Northern Song aesthetic toward the bold, heroic style of the Southern Song, prefiguring the patriotic school of poetry; his notable works include the collection 'Shilin Ci' and the poem 'He Xin Lang'. He is recognized in literary history as a polymath and a pivotal figure in the evolution of Song Dynasty Ci poetry.
刘一止: Liu Yizhi (1078—1161), courtesy name Xingjian, was an official and writer of the Southern Song Dynasty. His career was marked by frequent demotions due to his outspoken criticism of the court, and his works, characterized by a vigorous and lofty style, are collected in the 'Tiaoxi Ji'. He holds a significant position in the literary scene of the early Southern Song period.
万俟咏: Moqi Yong (c. 1061–after 1129), courtesy name Yayan and pseudonym Daliang Ciyin, was a poet of the late Northern Song Dynasty. Skilled in composing original melodies, his lyrical style closely followed that of Liu Yong, characterized by detailed narrative techniques; he holds a significant position in the history of Song poetry.
丘为: Qiu Wei was a poet of the Tang Dynasty, spanning the High to Mid-Tang periods. Known for his longevity and his close friendships with renowned poets like Wang Wei and Liu Changqing, his work is characterized by a clear, natural style, particularly in his landscape and pastoral poetry. His representative work, 'Visiting the Recluse of West Mountain and Not Finding Him,' secures his place in the history of Tang poetry.
刘眘虚: Liu Shenxu was a poet during the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty, also known by his courtesy name Quanyi, and served as the magistrate of Xia County. His poetry is characterized by a refined and tranquil style, focusing on landscapes and pastoral themes, with works like 'Que Ti' being his most celebrated. He is recognized as an important figure in the High Tang landscape and pastoral poetry school.
严仁: Yan Ren, courtesy name Cishan and pseudonym Qiaoxi, was a native of Shaowu during the Southern Song Dynasty, known alongside Yan Yu and Yan Can as one of the 'Three Yans of Shaowu.' His poetry is characterized by a delicate and graceful style, often expressing themes of travel-weariness and personal sentiment; though few of his works survive, he remains a notable figure in the late Song literary landscape.
彭元逊: Peng Yuanxun was a Ci poet of the late Southern Song Dynasty, known by his courtesy name Xunfu and pseudonym Zizhi. His works, collected in the 'Quan Song Ci', are characterized by a delicate and elegant style influenced by the Jiang Kui and Zhang Yan school, securing him a notable place in the history of late Song poetry.
陈克: Chen Ke (1081—1137), courtesy name Zigao, styled Chicheng Jushi, was a native of Linhai during the Southern Song Dynasty. Having served as a revision official at the Edict Bureau, he is known for his elegant and graceful poetry influenced by the Jiangxi School, holding a notable place in Song Dynasty literature; his works are preserved in the 'Chicheng Ji'.
王安石: Wang Anshi (1021-1086), courtesy name Jiefu, pseudonym Banshan, was a prominent statesman, thinker, and writer of the Northern Song Dynasty, and one of the 'Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song'. He implemented far-reaching reforms, and his literary style is characterized by vigor, depth, and precision, with his historical reflections and landscape poetry holding a significant place in literary history.
陈与义: Chen Yuyi (1090-1139), courtesy name Qufei and pseudonym Jianzhai, was a prominent poet of the early Southern Song Dynasty and the final master of the Jiangxi School of Poetry. His style evolved from elegant and delicate to profound and melancholic, with a mastery of seven-character regulated verse that captured the sorrow of displacement and patriotism, as seen in his famous work 'Climbing the Yueyang Tower'.
俞国宝: Yu Guobao was a scholar at the Imperial Academy during the Chunxi era of the Southern Song Dynasty. He gained fame for inscribing the poem 'Bu Suanzi' on a screen in a West Lake tavern, which caught the attention of Emperor Gaozong and led to his official career; his poetry is noted for its fresh style and remains a celebrated anecdote in the history of Song Ci.
